TECHNICAL INFORMATION LETTER
F-CLASS TURBINE WHEEL INSPECTION AND MAINTENANCE RECOMMENDATIONS
APPLICATION
Select F-class gas turbine rotors operating in high ambient and specific environmental conditions.
PURPOSE
Advise users to perform routine inspections at a maintenance interval based on installed configuration.
This TIL supersedes TILs 1280, 1327, 1434, 1539, 1540, and 1742.
REASON FOR REVISION
1) Added a new 3 Step-Age Heat Treatment category for Stage 1 & Stage 2 wheels.
2) Added a specific ECI inspection interval for Stage 1 enhanced wheels with 2 Step-Age heat treatment.
3) Added a specific ECI inspection interval for Stage 2 wheels post Rotor Life Extension.

BACKGROUND DISCUSSION
The function of the turbine rotor in a heavy-duty gas turbine engine includes carrying turbine blade loads, transmitting torque to
the compressor and generator for power generation, as well as supplying the turbine blades with cooling air. Prior to assembly,
the individual disks or wheels are balanced by the addition of weights installed in a groove. The weights are held in place by
deforming the metal on either the balance weight or the balance weight groove. The turbine blades are retained axially by a snap
ring type lock wire that is located in a machined groove passing through the turbine blades and turbine wheel. The portion of the
wheel retaining the lock wire is known as the lock wire tab. The F-class turbine blade cooling air supply is provided through
cooling slots in the bottom of the stage 1 and 2 turbine wheel dovetails.
Wheel
A-A
Figure 1: F-class Turbine Rotor Features
The disks in the turbine rotor are made of a high nickel alloy that is sensitive to surface imperfections where an intergranular
crack may initiate and propagate due to high stresses and temperatures. Depending on the initiation location, an undetected
crack may continue to propagate due to exposure to stress and temperature until either: 1- the crack is detected and either
repaired or the rotor is removed from service, or 2- the crack propagates to a critical length, releasing a wheel section and/or
adjacent turbine blades into the turbine hot gas path section potentially resulting in significant damage. Continuous improvements
have been made to the turbine rotor wheels over time in order to improve their overall damage sensitivity.
Rotors operating in high ambient and humid or corrosive conditions have an increased risk of crack initiation and propagation.
Recommended inspections and inspection intervals to mitigate crack propagation are provided based on wheel features, such as
shot peening condition at first fire, cooling slot geometry, material heat treatment, and environmental conditions. In some cases,
rotors may be swapped from site to site in order to expedite an outage. This TIL is being issued to all users in high ambient
and/or corrosive environmental conditions in order to provide recommendations for the various configurations.

Shot Peening Effect
Early generation turbine rotors have the highest sensitivity to surface imperfections. These rotors were manufactured and fired
without full shot peen coverage of the turbine wheels. Shot peening leaves a residual compressive stress and decreases the risk
of initiating a crack. Wheels that operated without shot peening have an increased risk of initiating and propagating a crack in the
rim region of the turbine rotor and in the turbine wheel dovetail slots. After 1996, all F-class turbine wheels shipped with full
peening coverage; these wheels were never fired without shot peening.
Cooling Slot
During operation, the intersection of the cooling slot and dovetail slot is subjected to high temperatures and tensile stresses
caused by turbine blade pull. The high temperatures and stresses in conjunction with an adverse edge condition have been
known to initiate cracks in this location.
Crack
Figure 2: Crack at Broached Wheel Post and Original Cooling Slot Corner
Three cooling slot shapes exist including original, contoured, and enhanced. The contoured (released in 2002) and enhanced
(released in 2006) cooling slot shapes were developed to lower stresses in the region where indications have been observed in
original slot configuration wheels. Please see Tables 1 and 2 below for eddy current inspection recommendations for original,
contour, and enhanced cooling slot configuration wheels. Some rotors may have a combination of enhanced, contoured, and/or
original configuration wheels, depending on rotor repair history. All wheels should follow their applicable inspection
recommendations. If a cooling slot crack is detected during the inspection, immediate wheel replacement will be recommended to
help avoid the risk of wheel post liberation during operation.

Lock Wire Tabs
Lock-wire tab (LWT) cracks have also been detected on the turbine rotor wheels. These types of cracks can typically be repaired
on site, subject to repair limits, without the need for rotor disassembly or wheel replacement.
Lockwire tab
crack
Stage 1
Wheel
Figure 4: Potential LWT Crack Orientations
Lock wire tab cracks may form in the upper corner of the lock wire tab groove, as shown in Figure 4. Cracks in this corner may
be caused by either:
Damage sustained during turbine blade installation/removal
High stresses in the lock wire fillet
GE Vernova has developed specialized procedures and tooling to help mitigate the risk of damage to the wheel lock wire tabs
during turbine blade installation and removal. These operations should always be performed by GE Vernova turbine blade
technicians to ensure the appropriate blade installation and removal tools and techniques are utilized. Modified or back cut
turbine blades reduce turbine blade loading into the tab. Wheels manufactured today have the extra fir trees removed in order to
avoid turbine blade loading in the tab altogether, as shown in Figure 5.

Balance Weight Groove
Cracking has been observed on several rotors at the balance weight groove (BWG) during routine inspections (Figure 6). It has
been found that this cracking initiated at an adverse edge condition because of the variability in the balance weight retention
method or at a location where the wheel surface was affected by an assembly or disassembly process that may have locally
altered the stress state. Cracks in the forward wheel web, if left unaddressed, could result in a partial wheel material liberation,
particularly when located on the stage 1 wheel.
Figure 6: Balance Weight Groove Stake Mark Cracking
Production turbine wheels have been improved, such that the balance weight groove is no longer staked or peened to deform
material around the balance weight. The stakeless balance rail can be seen in Figure 7.

Material Heat Treatment
Recently, a new heat treatment - designated as three-step-age (3SA) vs two-step-age (2SA) previously - was implemented. It
creates "engineered grain boundaries" that improve the hold-time fatigue capability of the turbine wheel alloy.
RECOMMENDATIONS
Units addressed by this communication have been identified as operating in a specific environment resulting in increased risk.
Event prevention and rotor health is best maintained through regular maintenance and inspections. Tables below provide
recommended inspections based on the turbine rotor shot peening condition and geometric features. In addition to these
inspections, it is recommended that back cut turbine blades always be installed on all turbine rotors.

Visual (VT), Borescope (BI), and Ultrasonic (UT)
A visual inspection of all exposed turbine rotor surfaces is recommended for all non-shot peened rotors; however, it is a good
practice for all users to evaluate the surface of their rotor when available. In order to complete a visual inspection, observe and
borescope all of the accessible rotor surfaces. Specifically, look for overall surface conditions such as dents, dings, nicks,
scratches, crack-like indications, raised material, etc.
Key features to examine:
Broach slot fillets, slot bottoms, tangs, and cooling slots (Visual)
Turbine blade cooling slots in wheel broach slots (Visual/BI)
Spacer rim seal tooth rubs/coating (Visual)
Balance weights: looseness/migration, staking quality, tight set screw (Visual/BI)
Nut damage or surface indications in flanges and webs (BI)
Counterbore outside diameter ligaments on distance piece and turbine aft shaft (UT)
Fluorescent Penetrant Inspection
Fluorescent penetrant inspection (FPI) is recommended to detect cracks on balance weights and lockwire tabs. However, it is
not recommended for the wheel posts, as cracks under the dovetail tangs are typically closed.
Recommended features to inspect:
Staked balance weight grooves: at all major inspection intervals and when the CDC is removed during a Hot Gas Path
inspection.
Lock wire tab fillets: When turbine blades are removed during routine maintenance intervals.
If crack-like indications are found, please contact your local GE Vernova service representative for disposition. In most cases, an
in-situ repair procedure can be used to remove cracked lock wire tabs or balance weight stake marks. A few isolated instances
have occurred where wheel replacement was necessary as the repair limits were exceeded.
Eddy Current Inspection
GE Vernova has developed an ECI method with advanced detection devices and techniques for turbine dovetail inspection
(Figure 8). This method is currently the most effective non-destructive test (NDT) for identifying indications in the wheel
dovetails.

Dovetail ECI should be performed until rotor retirement at the frequency defined in Table 1. ECI is available and recommended
for all wheel posts identified in Table 1 and 2. Third stage wheel posts and turbine wheels with any cooling slot configuration may
also be inspected with the same equipment, if elected.
Prior to the ECI, the turbine rotor must be appropriately cleaned to facilitate proper functioning of the ECI equipment and accurate
readings. A preferred method for cleaning is by dry ice (CO₂) blasting. This cleaning typically requires a single 12-hour shift to
clean the rotor after turbine blade removal and also requires the surfaces be free of oil beforehand. In the event that CO₂ blast is
not available, a more arduous and lengthy hand-cleaning process is acceptable (2-3 shifts). The rotor inspection then takes
approximately three shifts (~32 hours) to complete Stages 1 and 2. Both the rotor cleaning (performed by qualified vendor) and
the turbine rotor inspection can be scheduled through your local GE Vernova representative.
Modified Stage 1 and 2 Turbine Blades
The potential for crack initiation at the cooling slot location and lock wire tabs can be improved by reducing the amount of turbine
blade load passing through this area of the wheel. GE Vernova has developed a turbine blade modification to change the load
distribution in the wheel post, thereby decreasing the stress level at the cooling slot. This modification is accomplished by
machining a tapered relief into the turbine blade dovetail pressure faces adjacent to the cooling slot (see Figure 9). This relief is
often referred to as a dovetail "back cut." Relief cut modifications have been incorporated into new production F-class turbine
blades.

Qualified vendor to perform CO₂ blast cleaning of turbine rotor.
GE Vernova qualified personnel to perform rotor inspections.

turbine blade removal and installation should be four shifts (two days). These durations are estimates only.
